w:r.w:t: Parameter Density Estimation in Dynamical Systems

is a well-established approach for estimating the probability density functions of simulator parameters, given a real-world dataset. Various simulation-based inference approaches rely on neural density estimators and follow a so-called amortized inference strategy. The main idea is to perform a—potentially computationally costly—offline training procedure and to amortize this “invest” by fast and computationally cheap online evaluations of the neural density estimator
. While neural amortized inference approaches are starting to mature in

settings with black-box simulations and independent, identically distributed data points, there is still significant potential to leverage their advantages in other inference tasks. In particular, time-series data generated from dynamical systems exhibits a conditionally dependent structure, and the underlying system can usually be considered Markovian. These (and other) properties are exploited in some initial works to tailor amortized SBI methods in dynamical systems [2

The goal of this thesis is to analyze the potential of recent amortized SBI methods for online parameter density estimation in real-world systems, and to extend these methods, for instance, to cope with incomplete state observations.
To this end, a baseline neural density estimator,
such as neural posterior estimation (NPE) [1], and a state-of-the-art neural density estimator for time-series data, such as

neural posterior score estimation (NPSE) [2,3], should be implemented and compared against each other in a case study. Moreover, an extension of the state-of-the-art amortized SBI method for hidden Markov models should be investigated.
A promising strategy, formulated in [3, Sec. 5.2], is to use data assimilation strategies [4] within an NPSE framework.
In particular, the following tasks arise:
NPE, NPSE, and related amortized SBI approaches for time-series data
Implementation of a baseline and a state-of-the-art amortized SBI method
Comparison and analysis of their potential for parameter inference in representative case studies with dynamical systems that exhibit a Markovian property.
